questions.hint: Answer based on your requirement, not your current setup. Public endpoints on Confluent Cloud are authenticated and encrypted.

false → No, public endpoints are fine

questions.prompt: Do you need to move your existing data?

false → No, we can start fresh — Points producers and consumers at the new cluster and lets the old one retire

questions.prompt: Can your Schema Registry reach Confluent Cloud to sync schemas (outbound, port 443)?
Do any of your topics use non-default settings?
questions.hint: This includes retention over 7 days, a replication factor other than 3, a max message size over 2 MB, or a cleanup policy that combines compact and delete.

questions.prompt: Does your workload exceed any of the following: 1,920 megabytes/sec ingress, 5,760 megabytes/sec egress, or 240,000 requests per second?
Which cloud should your new Confluent Cloud cluster run on?
questions.hint: This is independent of your source cloud. Confluent supports cross-cloud migrations.

questions.prompt: Which authentication methods should your Confluent Cloud cluster support? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: A cluster can support several at once. On AWS we keep your existing mTLS as-is; on Azure and GCP, mTLS needs a Dedicated cluster, which we plan with you. OAuth and API keys are always set up new.

questions.prompt: How much coordination will it take to cut over all your clients and apps at the same time?
Do any applications use exactly-once transactions and/or Kafka Streams?
Do you want to keep your connectors self-managed, or move them to Confluent-managed?
legend: self-managed → Keep self-managed — Continue to run your own Connect cluster, which is new infrastructure to stand up if you’re moving off MSK Connect
confluent-managed → Move to Confluent-managed — Confluent runs the connector for you — no Connect cluster to stand up, scale, or patch  (default)

cluster_type.zone_reason: Spread across three Availability Zones, with an uptime SLA of up to 99.99% (at 2 or more eCKU). The cluster keeps serving through the loss of a zone.
cluster_type.reason: An Enterprise cluster fits your needs. You need private networking, which starts at Enterprise, and nothing else you told us pushes it up to Dedicated.
cluster_type.why: Private networking is required for your workload.
cluster_type.assessment_reason: Your answers point to Enterprise: private networking is a hard requirement for you, and that starts at Enterprise. Nothing else you told us pushes it up to Dedicated.

sizing.reason: We size from the most demanding of the numbers you gave us. Here that’s your partition count. This tier scales with your workload, so there is no capacity for you to pick.

networking.reason: On AWS, we recommend PNI (Private Network Interface) for your private connection. It scales to the full 32 eCKU, so it grows with you. Confluent Cloud pulls your data over the Cluster Link, reaching out to your source cluster. PNI doesn’t carry Cluster Linking traffic, so the link needs an Egress PrivateLink Endpoint alongside PNI.
networking.why: It scales to the full 32 eCKU, so it grows with you. The Egress PrivateLink Endpoint is added so the migration Cluster Link can reach your source cluster, which PNI doesn’t carry.
networking.how: PNI (Private Network Interface) is Confluent Cloud’s recommended private connection on AWS: Confluent Cloud attaches interfaces directly into your VPC, so traffic never crosses the public internet, and it scales to the full 32 eCKU (Confluent’s elastic capacity unit), the top of the Enterprise tier.
pros: Scales to the full 32 eCKU, the top of this tier
Traffic stays inside the Availability Zone when your clients are zone-aligned
networking.fit: AWS deployments that want the most room to grow

auth.reason: After cutover, your clients authenticate to Confluent Cloud with API keys (SASL/PLAIN). All credentials land as Confluent Cloud service accounts.
auth.why: Confluent Cloud issues new credentials for this method after cutover.

switchover.reason: We recommend a Cluster Linking cutover. At cutover you stop your producers, let the link finish, then restart them against Confluent Cloud, when you are ready rather than all at once. Your source credentials: No change. Cluster Linking uses your SCRAM credentials as-is.
switchover.how: Cluster Linking is Confluent Cloud’s built-in mirror: it copies your topics and offsets across continuously.

source_credential_handling.note: No change. Cluster Linking uses your SCRAM credentials as-is.

schema.reason: Your Confluent Platform Enterprise 7.1+ registry can reach Confluent Cloud, so we recommend Schema Linking. It preserves your schema IDs, and no client change is needed for the schema move.
schema.how: Schema Linking mirrors your schemas live from your source Schema Registry into Confluent Cloud Schema Registry.
pros: A live mirror that keeps Confluent Cloud in sync with your source
No client change needed for the schema move
cons: Your Schema Registry needs outbound reach to Confluent Cloud on port 443
The target Schema Registry is set to IMPORT mode
A dedicated context is needed if the target already holds schemas

connectors.reason: Connectors do not travel with your topics. Whichever way you go, you set each one up again on the other side. You are on MSK Connect today, so each connector is recreated as a Confluent-managed connector. Confluent’s Connect Migration Utility copies each connector’s configuration across, so you are not retyping them.

topics.value: Topics should mirror as they are
topics.reason: You told us your topics use Confluent Cloud’s defaults, so they carry over as they are. This cluster uses tiered storage, so view the historical-data decision for your backfill approach.

historical_data.reason: You need your consumer history, so Cluster Linking backfills your full tiered history. Your backfill time scales with peak tiered volume divided by sustained Cluster Linking throughput.

human_assist.reason: Your answers land inside what we can plan. This plan is yours to run. Talk to us if you want a second opinion.
